« Tu veux des frites ? » Au cours de l’h: “Want some fries?” During the lunch hour at Jean-Grou secondary school in Rivière-des-Prairies, many people cross paths with Riguerre Antoine and say hello. Some even offer him a taste of what they just bought at the IGA across from the school.

Riguerre is known by the young people in his corner of the island for good reason: he has more than 25 years of experience working with youth in Rivière-des-Prairies.
Un mercredi midi comme un autre. La cloc: A Wednesday noon like any other. The bell at Jean-Grou secondary school rings, signalling the lunch break. Close to the school, Riguerre Antoine pulls on his fluorescent yellow safety vest, which makes him visible among the crowd of teenagers heading out to eat.
La patrouille s’amorce. À l’occasion, de: The patrol begins. Now and then, young people greet him or nod when they see him. “I like to describe myself as just a citizen of Rivière-des-Prairies,” Riguerre says as he walks. The 47-year-old arrived in Montréal from Haiti in 1985 and grew up in the neighbourhood. “I’m a kid from here. I did my elementary school, my high school and my CEGEP in the neighbourhood,” he says.
Au début de l’âge adulte, Riguerre assis: At the start of adulthood, Riguerre witnessed and took part in the founding of <l1>Équipe RDP, an organization dedicated to social development and to improving the quality of life of the population of Montréal and its surrounding areas by offering recreation and social intervention programs</l1>. He takes part in several prevention projects in which young people are at the heart of the organization’s goals.
Intervenant auprès des jeunes, pionnier: A youth worker, a pioneer of Équipe RDP, a former high school coordinator and a rapper in his spare time, Riguerre wears many hats. Today, he presents himself as just an individual from his neighbourhood. Too humble to admit it, he is nonetheless seen here by some as a “legend,” a man who holds the streets of the island’s northeast in his heart.
En ce qui concerne Riguerre, il est impo: When it comes to Riguerre, it is important to understand that his path in the community trained him for the role of go-between for young people and the street. “It’s first and foremost the bonds I have with the people in my neighbourhood that got me where I am today. It’s not my schooling or anything else, it’s really who I am to these people,” he explains.
<strong>La réalité de l’est de l’île</st: The reality of the east end of the island
C’est en connaissant sa communauté que R: It is by knowing his community that Riguerre reaches it and has real influence. “I know the difficulties the young people here will go through, especially young people from immigrant families and young people who, like me, come from the HLMs of Rivière-des-Prairies,” he says. “When you know your people, you know how to help them. You know what they need, and you know how to adapt your approach to them.”
Ce qui distingue son quartier du reste d: According to the youth worker, what sets his neighbourhood apart from the rest of the city is the mistaken perception people have of it. “RDP is a rich neighbourhood. If you go down Gouin, there are huge houses on the waterfront, and if you go a little farther, there are HLMs. It’s a rich neighbourhood with pockets of poverty,” he explains. “When you look at the average income by neighbourhood, it doesn’t reflect the inequalities that exist between the richest and the poorest,” he says indignantly.
Amoureux de son quartier, il n’ignore to: He loves his neighbourhood, but he is not blind to the problems that plague the streets where he spent his teenage years.
« Durant les années 1990, le lieu de ras: “In the 1990s, the gathering place par excellence was the street,” recalls the Rivière-des-Prairies native. “There were problems linked to young people. I don’t want to use the term ‘street gang,’ because I think it was above all a lack of activities and opportunities for young people that created certain problems,” he adds.
Une autre réalité du quartier, c’est que: Another reality of the neighbourhood is that it is a “bedroom community,” says the man in his forties. “It’s like a kind of residential suburb. The people who make a lot of money don’t work in the neighbourhood. They go off to work in Laval, across the bridge, or downtown, and then come back here to relax and spend the night. They don’t live here,” he explains.
Mais qu’en est-il des autres habitants d: But what about the neighbourhood’s other residents? “There’s another ‘clientele,’” says Riguerre. “There are the ones who live here, who send their kids to the local public schools. They might be the ones facing certain difficulties.”
“There’s almost nothing for our youth. It’s a suburb-type neighbourhood,” he repeats. “There’s little or no infrastructure for young people. You go home to sleep, you’ve got your pool, you’ve got your own stuff, but you don’t have arcades, you don’t have a movie theatre, you don’t have those kinds of places and spaces.”
Il devient donc normal, estime l’interve: It is therefore natural, the youth worker believes, that young people with no access to anything outside the neighbourhood feel isolated and abandoned.

Après avoir été pendant plus d’une vingt: After spending more than twenty years with a front-row seat to what is happening among young people, Riguerre believes they are poorly represented when it comes to the neighbourhood’s problems. “It’s like in a high school. If 5% of the kids cause problems, from the outside, people will think all the kids in the school are a problem,” he compares.
En d’autres mots, l’intervenant croit qu: In other words, the youth worker believes this generalization is one of the causes of young people’s isolation and of their mistrust of the institutions that are supposed to serve and protect them.
« Il y a une partie des jeunes qui sont: “Some young people are, in a way, kept on track by sports or other extracurricular activities, but there is still a small portion of teenagers who don’t feel drawn to any of that,” he continues. “The fact is that the ones who aren’t interested in anything else end up with a lot of free time. How do we provide structure for those kids?” he asks.
Il faut être réaliste : certains ne veul: We have to be realistic: some don’t want structure, says the Montrealer. “Not from a youth centre, not from a sports team, not from school,” he lists. Drawing on his personal experience, he adds that he has known many young people who lacked motivation. “It’s always been a minority, but by associating them with all the young people in the neighbourhood, you marginalize all the young people in the neighbourhood,” he insists.
Comment remédier à cette situation et ai: How can this situation be remedied and this “at-risk” minority helped? The citizen points out that certain negative stereotypes must not be generalized. For example, when activities are organized, youth workers take care to make them for all young people, not just some of them. “We do activities for young people, period. Not for vulnerable youth, not for disadvantaged youth, just for youth. It promotes inclusion and prevents some from becoming isolated,” he explains.
« La force des organismes, c’est la prox: “The strength of community organizations is their closeness to people,” he says he has noticed over the years. “It’s harder for officials who work with the City, for example, to understand people’s needs in the neighbourhoods, because there’s a certain distance.” As mentioned above, the greater presence of youth workers in the community makes it possible to build a healthier relationship between organizations and the street. “We want to create opportunities for young people the community has a hard time bringing into its activities,” he says.
Riguerre explique que, dans la vie d’un: Riguerre explains that in a young person’s life, there are two places where they spend most of their time: school and home. “School is a living environment with significant adults who should be able to identify young people’s potential and adapt the school program accordingly. That’s why we have to find a way to make it appealing to them,” he breaks down. “It should be fun to go to school,” he says with feigned irony, given that many young people see school as a chore.
« Je pense à des jeunes que je connais p: “I think of young people I know personally who aren’t interested in school. For these kids who have nowhere to spend their free time between school and home, chilling outside becomes almost a must. By being out in the field and on patrol after school and at lunchtime, youth workers create a kind of bridge in the street, a stopover,” he says.
« Chaque jeune aura à faire un travail p: “Every young person will have personal work to do,” he finally says. Fascinated himself by the question of identity, the Rivière-des-Prairies resident has only one piece of advice for the youngest: they should seek to “find their identity again.”
Ces paroles ne sont pas anodines, surtou: These words are not trivial, especially coming from a second-generation immigrant. Even though he only arrived here at the age of nine, Riguerre understands the questions tied to immigration and to the search for identity when you are part of a visible minority.
Il n’y a pas d’âge pour tenter de compre: There is no age limit for trying to understand who we are and where we come from. At 47, Riguerre says it loud and clear: “Social ills mean that if society is sick, it has an impact on young people.”
